slides.title: What is an API?
slides.narration:
What if I told you that different computer programs can talk to each other?
An **API**, or Application Programming Interface, makes this possible.
It acts like a messenger.
Think of an **API** like a waiter in a restaurant.
You give your order to the waiter.
The waiter takes it to the kitchen.
The kitchen prepares your food.
The waiter then brings your food back to you.
Similarly, an **API** takes your request to a service and brings back the response.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration showing API as a messenger between two programs, with a waiter serving food

slides.title: What is an API Key?
slides.narration:
How does a service know it's you making the request?
This is where an **API key** comes in.
An **API key** is a unique secret code.
It identifies you and proves you are allowed to access a service.
Imagine it as your ID card to enter a special club.
Only members with an ID card can place orders.
Always keep your **API key** private and secure.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration of an API key as an ID card unlocking access to a service

slides.title: Making an API Request
slides.narration:
You now know what an **API** is and how an **API key** works.
Let us see how to make an **API request**.
An **API request** is like placing an order to a service.
It includes your **API key** for authentication.
It also includes your instruction or prompt.
The **API** then sends this request to the model.
The model processes your instruction.
Finally, the **API** returns the output to you.
Let's see this in action with a grocery app example.
Open any grocery app on your phone.
Tap the search bar at the top.
Type 'tomato' and press **Enter**.
The app sends an **API request** to the server.
The request asks for products matching 'tomato'.
The server processes this request.
It sends back a list of matching products.
Then, the app displays these products on your screen.
slides.image_prompt: Person using a grocery app on a phone, typing 'tomato' in search bar

slides.title: Vague API Request
slides.narration:
Now, let us try making different types of **API requests**.
First, consider a vague **API request**.
This type of request asks for general information.
It lacks specific details.
For example, asking an **AI** model, 'Tell me about cars.'
This will likely give you a broad, unspecific response.
It will not be very helpful.
slides.image_prompt: Screen close-up: user typing 'Tell me about cars...'

slides.title: Improved API Request
slides.narration:
Let's see how to make a better **API request**.
An improved **API request** is precise.
It provides clear context.
For example, you could ask to summarize key features of electric cars in 3 bullet points.
Focus on their environmental impact and performance.
This guides the **AI** model.
It provides a targeted and useful response.
slides.image_prompt: Screen close-up: user typing 'Summarize key features of electric cars in 3 bullet points...'

slides.title: Comparing API Request Results
slides.narration:
Let us compare the results of these two requests.
The vague request gave a generic overview.
The improved request provided specific, actionable information.
It was relevant to what we needed.
Clear and precise prompts lead to much better **AI** outputs.
Understanding this helps you get the most from **AI** tools.
slides.image_prompt: Side-by-side: vague prompt output vs improved prompt output

slides.title: APIs in Real Life: A Grocery App
slides.narration:
You just saw how an improved request works.
Let us revisit our grocery app example.
When you search for an item, say 'tomato':
The app sends an **API request** to the server.
The server processes your request.
It fetches data from its database.
It then sends this data back to your app.
Finally, the products appear on your screen.
This seamless interaction is entirely powered by **APIs**.
slides.image_prompt: Seamless interaction of a grocery app showing 'tomato' search results, powered by APIs

slides.title: Summary
slides.narration:
Let us summarize what we learned.
We defined **APIs** as messengers.
We understood **API keys** for authentication.
We learned how to make effective **API requests**.
We also saw a real-life application example.

slides.title: Assignment
slides.narration:
Now as an assignment,
Think of another everyday application.
Identify how **APIs** might be used within it.
Describe the request and response flow.
Compare the results.
